newsitem.title: USA: US HRW wheat ratings improve, but caution urged.
newsitem.headline: US HRW wheat ratings improve, but caution urged.

text.p: U.S. winter wheat conditions improved during the week ended April 27, but agronomists said the damage from April's freeze may not be known until harvest.
Overall, winter wheat improved to 58 percent good to excellent from 46 percent the previous week, according to a summary of state agricultural statistics service reports.

KANSAS - Freeze damage was limited to the southern areas, while damage elsewhere did not appear as severe as earlier assessments indicated. "The (freezing) temperatures we had should have just blistered it, but they didn't," said Jim Shroyer, a Kansas State University extension agronomist.
"I would say at this time 40 million (bushels) is gone, but at harvest time it could be 60 million."
Initial estimates put freeze damage at 100 million bushels or more. Before the freeze, the state was expected to produce 400 million bushels.

Shroyer said many freeze-hit fields remained green and continued to grow, which may have misled crop scouts into believing the wheat was in better shape than it really was. He said damaged tillers that remained green may yet die.
Kansas wheat was upgraded this past week to 55 percent good to excellent from 40 percent the previous week.

In Garfield County, a top wheat producer in north central Oklahoma, headed wheat that was thought to be dead was pollinating, said Ron Robinson, the county's agriculture agent. "That looks real promising," he said, but warned more development was needed to assess the crop's condition.
"If we have four or five warm days, we will know (the extent of damage) in a hurry," he said.

As of Sunday, Oklahoma's wheat was rated 29 percent good to excellent, 36 fair, 23 poor and 12 very poor. Before the freeze, some grain merchandisers estimated a wheat crop of 180 million bushels versus last year's harvest of 93.1 million.

TEXAS - In the High Plains, dryland fields sustained greater damage than irrigated fields, and headed fields in the north central region exhibited freeze damage. Damage to late boot fields may not be as severe as earlier indicated.
As of Sunday, the crop was rated 24 percent good to excellent, 39 fair, 26 poor and 11 very poor.

WASHINGTON - Winter wheat in southwest Lewis County appeared stressed by cool weather. In Kittitas County in central Washington, about half the dryland winter wheat succumbed to root rot and other damage because of extremely long snow cover and wet late winter and spring conditions.
Dryland winter wheat was rated 59 percent good to excellent, 35 fair and six poor. Irrigated wheat was rated 95 percent good to excellent and five fair.
